title: Climate misinformation and quoted liquidity in energy equities

author.affiliation: Department of Government, University of Essex

abstract: Does climate misinformation predict trading costs in energy equities? This paper combines a sector-specific content index from 217,954 English-language Facebook posts with daily financial data. The principal sample contains 485,800 observations on 202 securities in nine energy sub-industries during January 2012–October 2025. A fixed language-model rubric scores misinformation and sector relevance separately. Positive spread associations under monthly controls change sign when market-by-date and sector-by-month fixed effects are included on a common sample. The principal specification uses prior-session financial controls and yields a coefficient of -0.0014 percentage points per index point (approximate 95% sector/date-clustered interval [-0.0065, 0.0036]). A sample-standard-deviation difference in content corresponds to -0.102 basis points in spread, with an interval of [-0.462, 0.258]. Alternative inference and timing checks do not establish a stable positive liquidity-cost association. The observational design, nine sector clusters, unvalidated classifier accuracy, and absence of observed investor exposure limit interpretation. The findings show why sector-level content measures require local market controls and explicit measurement checks before being interpreted as the financial costs of climate misinformation.
